72d6c62c9048: What does the word “remonstrated” most nearly mean in this passage?
Scrooge objects that he is “a mortal” who is “liable to fall,” so he is protesting against going out the window.
Why does the narrator list the cold weather, the warm bed and Scrooge's light clothing?
They are excuses Scrooge might give for not going
They show Scrooge is ready for a trip
They describe a cozy, happy night
They explain why Scrooge cannot sleep
The narrator says “It would have been in vain for Scrooge to plead” these things, so they are reasons he would like to stay behind.
What does the Spirit's grasp, “gentle as a woman's hand,” show about its power?
It is gentle but impossible to refuse
It is weak and easy to escape
Though gentle, “The grasp … was not to be resisted,” so Scrooge has no choice but to rise.
240fd0af1fe2: According to the last paragraph, what really warmed and fed Becky?
The narrator says “Something else had warmed and fed her, and the something else was Sara.”
Why would Becky no longer mind the heavy coal boxes?
Sara's story would give her something happy to think about
Sara promised to carry the coal for her
The cook had stopped being cruel
She would soon leave her job
Becky says she wouldn't mind “HOW heavy the coal boxes was … if—if I might have that to think of.”
What does the word “devoutly” suggest about how Becky speaks?
With deep, sincere feeling, almost like a prayer
Becky “breathed … devoutly,” showing how deeply she longs to hear the rest of the story.
f688ff310422: What is the main conflict in this scene?
A bitter argument over respect for church leaders
A dispute over who will carve the meat
A quarrel about the price of the dinner
A disagreement about where to spend Christmas
Dante insists on “respect for the pastors of the church,” while Mr Dedalus mocks them as a “tub of guts.”
How does Mr Dedalus attack the bishop he mentions?
By mocking him with crude insults and imitation
By calmly listing his political errors
By refusing to speak about him at all
He calls him a “Tub of guts” and makes “a grimace of heavy bestiality” with “a lapping noise with his lips.”
What is the tone of Mr Casey's phrase “Princes of the church”?
Mr Casey says it “with slow scorn,” turning Dante's praise into mockery.
ffe9c247d83b: What does the simile “a face like a fine mask” suggest about the man?
His true feelings are hidden behind a fixed, controlled expression
He is wearing a costume for a party
He is kind and open with everyone
The face has “one set expression on it,” and only the nostrils show “the only little change that the face ever showed.”
What do the slight changes in the man's nostrils reveal?
When the dints change, “they gave a look of treachery, and cruelty, to the whole countenance.”
What contrast does the description create?
The man is handsome on the surface but sinister underneath
The man is ugly but secretly gentle
The man is poor but proud
The man is young but looks old
Despite the hint of cruelty, the narrator says “it was a handsome face, and a remarkable one.”
846dfb35571e: Why does Alice say “Curiouser and curiouser!”?
She is so surprised that she forgets how to speak properly
She is trying to make a joke
She wants to teach a new word
She is reading from a book
The narrator says “she was so much surprised, that for the moment she quite forgot how to speak good English.”
What does Alice mean when she says she is “opening out like the largest telescope”?
She is growing very tall very fast
She can see very far away
She is looking through a telescope
Her feet “seemed to be almost out of sight, they were getting so far off,” so her body is stretching out like a telescope.
Why does Alice decide to be kind to her feet?
She worries they might not walk where she wants
She thinks her feet are crying
She wants to sell her boots
Her feet are cold from the snow
Alice thinks, “I must be kind to them … or perhaps they won’t walk the way I want to go!”
51b779e57ab3: What is Major's central message in his speech?
Animals must unite because humans are their enemies
Animals and humans should work as partners
Animals should obey their human masters
Each animal should look out only for itself
Major declares “All men are enemies. All animals are comrades.”
What does the incident with the rats and dogs suggest right after Major's speech?
The animals' 'perfect unity' is not as easy as Major claims
The dogs are guarding the rats
The rats are working for the humans
Major asks for “perfect unity, perfect comradeship,” yet the dogs at once chase the rats, which escape only “by a swift dash for their holes.”
What does the word “falter” most nearly mean in this passage?
Major warns that “your resolution must never falter” and that “No argument must lead you astray,” so falter means to weaken.
05f2a508c37a: What does “her dauntless spirit subdued at last” suggest about Anne?
Anne is usually bold, but this upsets her badly
Anne is always timid and shy
Anne thinks the situation is funny
“Dauntless” means fearless, so for Anne's spirit to be “subdued at last” shows how upset the scarlet nose makes her.
Why does Diana hesitate before speaking?
She is nervous about telling Anne something embarrassing
She has forgotten what she wanted to say
She is angry about the feathers
She wants Anne to guess a riddle
Diana stammers “It . . . it . . . isn’t the feathers” before admitting “it’s . . . your nose, Anne.”
What does the phrase “the fatal truth” add to the scene?
It makes a small problem sound like a dramatic disaster, for humour
It shows Anne is in real danger
It means Anne has broken the mirror
It shows the story is a tragedy
Calling a red nose “the fatal truth” exaggerates the moment when “Her nose was a brilliant scarlet!”
0b5782c483f0: What does Matthew think about Marilla's way of dressing Anne?
He trusts Marilla but thinks one pretty dress would do no harm
He thinks Marilla is cruel and wrong
He wants Anne to dress plainly forever
He has no opinion about clothes
He thinks “Marilla knew best” but also “surely it would do no harm to let the child have one pretty dress.”
What does the phrase “putting in of his oar” most nearly mean?
Doing his share of farm work
Matthew hopes a gift “surely could not be objected to as an unwarranted putting in of his oar,” meaning he doesn't want to meddle in Marilla's job.
How does Matthew feel after making his decision?
He acts “with a sigh of satisfaction” as he puts away his pipe and goes to bed.
ecd66b7b19aa: Why does Mr. Fogg order the ship's interior to be burned?
To provide dry wood to keep the steam engine running
To destroy evidence of a crime
The narrator explains, “It was necessary to have dry wood to keep the steam up to the adequate pressure.”
What does Fogg's question “The vessel now belongs to me?” reveal about him?
He is calm and practical, thinking ahead to his plan
He is unsure whether he paid enough
He wants to become a sea captain
He is joking with the captain
Once told it is his “from the keel to the truck of the masts,” he immediately orders the seats and bunks pulled down and burned.
What does the phrase “a perfect rage for demolition” describe?
The crew's energetic, eager destruction of the ship
A storm tearing the ship apart
The crew “worked lustily,” and “Passepartout hewed, cut, and sawed away with all his might.”
cf9e7eb1e315: What does Abbleway first expect will happen to the woman?
He expects the wolves to kill her
He expects her to find shelter
He expects her to tame the wolves with food
He expects her to freeze in the snow
He hides his face because he “had no wish to see a human being torn to pieces and devoured before his eyes.”
Why is Abbleway “scandalised” rather than simply relieved?

He is jealous of the woman's courage
He thinks the woman cheated him
He is angry that the wolves ran away
He “had been straitly brought up in a small English town, and he was not prepared to be the witness of a miracle.”
What is ironic about the wolves' behaviour?
The feared wolves only play joyfully with the woman
The wolves run away in fear of the snow
Instead of attacking, the wolves only “drench her with snow as they gambolled round her,” and give “A short, joyous bark.”
8ad9c4414369: What is the mother horse's opinion of hunting?
She does not understand why men harm themselves and horses for it
She thinks hunting is exciting fun
She believes hunting is necessary for food
She wishes she could join the hunt

What does the detail that George was “the pride of his family” add to the scene?
It makes his accident feel even more tragic
It shows he was a careless rider
It explains why he won the hunt
It shows the family did not care
Being “the squire’s only son, a fine, tall young man” makes the loss deeply painful for his family.
78485631a662: According to Paine, where does America's great strength lie?
In unity rather than in numbers
Paine states, “It is not in numbers, but in unity, that our great strength lies.”
What does Paine mean by “the time hath found us”?
The right moment for action has clearly arrived
The colonists have wasted too much time
Britain has discovered the colonists' plans
He says “the inquiry ceases at once” because “The general concurrence, the glorious union of all things prove the fact.”

Waiting will make building a navy harder as timber disappears
Timber should be sold to Britain for profit
America has endless forests, so there is no hurry
Timber is useless for building ships

1992d4d31cc7: What illusion does the narrator say was destroyed?
That Frenchmen know good food when they see it
That the patron was a skilled cook
He writes that it “destroyed one of my illusions, namely, the idea that Frenchmen know good food when they see it.”

If this place counts as good, the bad ones must be terrible
Paris has the best restaurants in the world
All Paris restaurants are the same

7cf4fb2d9bbd: What is the dominant mood of this passage?
The narrator describes “a nervous suspense over us all” and says “The silence finally became agonising.”
What does the simile about the blood “like blows from a hammer” emphasize?
How intensely the narrator's own body reacts to the strain
That Renfield is hitting the wall
That the narrator has been injured

What does the word “Inured” most nearly mean here?
He was “Inured … to sick beds and death,” yet still “this suspense grew, and grew upon me,” showing how unusual the moment was.
6cd8c4d6b0a8: What does Eliza's memory of James's plan reveal?
He had a hopeful wish to revisit his childhood home that never came true
He had planned a long trip abroad
He wanted to buy Johnny Rush's business

What does the mistake “rheumatic wheels” suggest about Eliza?
She is simple and not well educated
She is making a clever joke
She knows a lot about carriages

What does Eliza gazing “into the empty grate” suggest?
Her grief and sense of emptiness after the death
That she is cold and wants a fire
That she is bored with the visitors
That she is looking for something she dropped

14c2afebc84e: What surprising fact about kings does Bacon point out?
They value friendship so highly they risk their own safety for it
They never need friends at all
They buy friends with gold coins
They forbid their subjects to have friends
Bacon notes kings “purchase it, many times, at the hazard of their own safety and greatness.”
Why, according to Bacon, can princes not easily enjoy friendship?
Their high position separates them from everyone else
They are too busy fighting wars
Their subjects refuse to speak to them

It is shorter than the modern names

9e6375bd0dbd: What does Lamb mean by saying he “had left the temple a devotee, and was returned a rationalist”?
He once saw the theatre with worshipful wonder but now sees it with cool reason
He has given up religion for science
He has stopped attending the theatre entirely
He has become an actor himself
Now “the emblem, the reference, was gone,” and the curtain is merely “a certain quantity of green baize.”
Where does Lamb finally locate the cause of his disappointment?
In the change within himself, not in the actors
In the poor quality of the actors
In the dull comedy being performed

It let him lower his expectations before seeing Mrs. Siddons
It made him laugh enough to forget his troubles
It let him leave the theatre early

4055625d66ae: What “nice thing” came from the four nasty things?
The narrator says the four nasty things “all joined together to bring one nice thing, and that was sleep.”
How do the children feel at the start of the passage?

What does it tell us that the sun had set when Anthea woke?

Anthea woke very early in the morning

When Anthea wakes, “The sun had set, and the twilight was coming on.”
65c065a52942: What does the repetition in “deep, dark, deathlike solitude” emphasize?
How extreme and gloomy Victor's isolation has become
That Victor enjoys a peaceful rest
That the night is very cold
That Victor is planning an escape
Victor “shunned the face of man” and found “solitude was my only consolation—deep, dark, deathlike solitude.”

Excessive grief harms both the survivors and Victor himself

7cc5f61a36d1: How do Herbert and the others show their care for the narrator?
They tear up their own handkerchiefs to make bandages
They carry him all the way home

“they tore up their handkerchiefs to make fresh bandages, and carefully replaced it in the sling.”

The darkness shows his growing fear
The moon shows he is lost

9bca8782e379: What is humorous about the food allowance for the 'man-mountain'?
It is calculated with absurd precision as enough for 1724 subjects

985197692b86: What is the main purpose of this passage?

To tell how Heidi's story ends

a45dea54dced: What does Orwell mean that his wife was being used “as a decoy duck”?

c09b613cfb30: How has Jane's feeling toward Mrs. Reed changed?

6bfd9a19607b: What does the phrase “hung upon the apex of disaster a single tremendous instant” emphasize?

b9de425ae540: What is Leacock's main purpose in this passage?
To humorously mock popular health habits like early rising and cold baths

7ecffc81b1d6: What is the overall mood of the picnic?

6e7895b08dec: What does Emma's silent watching of the turning wheels suggest about her mood?

f6bbeed1d3c2: Why do people stare at Ishmael and Queequeg?

17d5914a5bb7: What does the woman's reply show about her character?

“although he had been up in the cold nearly all night,” he would ride to Black Hawk “with no roads to guide him.”
c19894a30569: What central metaphor does Russell use for human life?

A ship sailing on calm seas
A race won by the strongest
